title: Why Is Jupiter Beside the Moon on November 30?
relatedVideoTitle: Why You Can't Stand On Jupiter
description:
On November 30, 2026 at 08:25 UTC, brilliant Jupiter passes just 1.05 degrees — about two full-Moon widths, or one finger held at arm's length — beside the waning gibbous Moon.

In the morning sky they look like neighbours. In reality, Jupiter (69,911 km radius — as big as a basketball if Earth were a grape) is 40 times wider than our Moon (1,740 km radius), yet appears as a bright point of light because it sits 754 million kilometres away compared with the Moon's 373,000 kilometres — more than 2,000 times farther into space. Look south before sunrise on November 30 to spot them side by side with the naked eye.

Watch the full Jupiter film next: Why You Can't Stand On Jupiter (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-jmMROGoZCM)

Sources: NASA/JPL Solar System Dynamics Horizons Ephemeris (ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/, 2026-11-30 08:25 UTC Moon 301 & Jupiter 599 geocentric ephemeris); Ernie Wright, 'Moon Phase and Libration, 2026', NASA Scientific Visualization Studio #5587 (svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5587); NASA Science, 'Jupiter Facts' (science.nasa.gov/jupiter/jupiter-facts/); NASA Science, 'Moon Facts' (science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/); NASA Science, 'What's Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA' (2026).

Image credits: NASA / JPL-Caltech / SwRI / MSSS (Juno PIA22946, PIA26077, PIA21974); NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (Ernie Wright, SVS #5587 unlabelled plain Moon visualizations); NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (GSFC_20171208_Archive_e002130, GSFC_20171208_Archive_e001939); NASA Johnson Space Center (Apollo 11 AS11-44-6667, ISS Expedition 70 ISS070-E-062746). Pictures: NASA imagery alongside our own scale graphics. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
